questions.prompt: Is the puck currently assigned to either team?
questions.explanation: The puck has no owner in this setup, matching the stated contested touch.

questions.prompt: Choose two reasons to avoid leaving too early.

options.text: Every loose puck will become a breakout

questions.explanation: Possession and remaining threats matter. A partner’s proximity is not proof of control.

questions.prompt: Arrange a cautious support read.

options.text: Check the remaining threat near the net
Move to support the outcome you actually see

questions.explanation: Checks can overlap; the important point is not assuming a win.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to balance net-side support with a possible outlet angle.
questions.explanation: A modest change can offer support while remaining between an inside attacker and the net. Multiple positions are defensible.

questions.prompt: D1 now controls the puck and Gold 1 skates past. What can you reassess?

options.text: Whether a loose-puck battle still exists unchanged
Whether Gold 2 has disappeared from the play
Whether to widen into a clear outlet

questions.explanation: Secure control may permit a wider support position, but Gold 2 still needs to be read.

questions.prompt: What visible sign would tell you this situation has become a breakout opportunity?
questions.explanation: Describe controlled possession and a usable next option, rather than simply seeing D1 near the puck.

questions.prompt: What remains unknown at this freeze?

options.text: Which team will control the bouncing puck

questions.explanation: The puck has no owner, so possession is unresolved; if D1 controls it, YOU supports breakout, while Gold control starts a defensive read.

questions.prompt: Which two cues should YOU communicate to D1?

options.text: Gold 1 is close to the next touch
The net-side support lane is covered or open
Tell D1 the puck is theirs before the contest is settled

questions.explanation: Pressure distance and inside support tell D1 whether to protect or move it; the bounce direction is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Move YOU slightly inside to support D1 while keeping the net between you and Gold 1.
questions.explanation: The inside support spot protects the net and leaves D1 the puck-side route; if Gold 1 wins it, step to the new carrier.

questions.prompt: What visible sign would change your job from partner support to breakout support?
questions.explanation: Clear control on D1’s stick changes the task from contest coverage to outlet and spacing; if the puck remains loose, keep the net-side lane protected.

questions.prompt: Which supporting role does the coach give F2?

options.text: A rush directly to the far net

questions.explanation: The role is stated in the briefing and is not inferred from a system name.

questions.prompt: What two features could make F2’s option different from F1’s?

options.text: A position closer to Navy’s net

questions.explanation: Different depth and angle can create another choice; a defender may still close it.

questions.prompt: Arrange a possible regroup support routine.

options.text: Adjust as D1 chooses a route

questions.explanation: The support routine is flexible and should respond to the puck.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into a deeper middle support example.
questions.explanation: This location gives D1 a different depth from F1. Check Gold 1 before treating it as a passing lane.

questions.prompt: Gold 1 moves directly onto your new lane. What might you do?

options.text: Rush beside F1 and remove the deeper option
Change the angle again or help clear F1’s route

questions.explanation: An option should be re-created when the marker moves.

questions.prompt: Why can two forwards at the same height make D1’s job harder?
questions.explanation: They may be covered by similar pressure and leave no release toward their own net. Spacing depends on defenders, not just symmetry.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call before dropping below F1?
questions.explanation: The call names the deeper middle support the coach assigned, giving D1 a different height to see; if Gold 1 closes that lane, call the next connected angle.

questions.prompt: Which two facts make a deeper route useful?

options.text: F1 is already high on the boards
D1 needs a different passing height

questions.explanation: F1’s high position and D1’s need for a different lane make the deeper route useful; overlap removes the separation.

questions.prompt: Move YOU below F1 into the coach-assigned middle support pocket.
questions.explanation: The lower-middle spot separates YOU from F1 and gives D1 a safer connection; if Gold 1 follows, preserve the lane behind the pressure.

questions.prompt: Why can two players at the same height make D1’s reset harder?
questions.explanation: They present one predictable line, allowing one defender to cover both, while different heights create a forward and backward choice; if one lane closes, the other can remain.

questions.prompt: Who has possession after the stated lateral pass?
questions.explanation: The setup assigns the puck to D2 and the briefing states the pass has ended.

questions.prompt: Pick two useful checks for your next support movement.

options.text: The angle for a return pass
Whether remaining level with D2 looks tidy

questions.explanation: A staggered option can help, but only if pressure and the return route permit it.

questions.prompt: Order one follow-up to this D-to-D pass.

options.text: Present an option and read the next pass

questions.explanation: These are suggested actions; do not delay necessary defensive support merely to finish a pattern.

questions.prompt: Move YOU beneath D2 to illustrate a return outlet.
questions.explanation: A deeper diagonal can separate the return route from the approaching forechecker. It is not an automatic passing instruction.

questions.prompt: If D2 sends the puck forward with control, what might your next job become?

options.text: Advance in support while checking defensive cover
Remain closer to Navy’s net than the old puck position indefinitely
Follow Gold 1 away from the developing play

questions.explanation: Support should follow the new location and possession quality, with cover retained.

questions.prompt: How is useful staggering different from simply standing far apart?
questions.explanation: Describe depth, a visible lane and pressure. Large separation without a usable connection may not help.

questions.prompt: What should YOU tell D2 as Gold 1 approaches?

options.text: I will stand on D2’s lane

questions.explanation: Calling the lower outlet gives D2 a connected escape from the approaching pressure; if D2 advances, re-read the next support lane rather than staying fixed.

questions.prompt: Which two facts should shape YOU’s follow-up?

options.text: YOU can be a lower outlet

questions.explanation: Pressure and a lower outlet give D2 a connected next action; matching height makes the reset flat.

questions.prompt: Move YOU below D2 to show the requested return outlet.
questions.explanation: The lower position gives D2 a backward safety valve and keeps Gold 1’s approach visible; if D2 advances, YOU can support the next lane.

questions.prompt: How is staggering different from simply moving away from D2?
questions.explanation: Staggering changes the passing height and keeps a connected lane, while random distance can leave D2 with no useful angle; if pressure changes, adjust the stagger.

In this exercise the first support option is a controlled middle route toward the far-post area. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: F1 carries in a wide lane near the side boards.

questions.prompt: Which side is F1 using for the entry?
questions.explanation: F1 carries in a wide lane near the side boards.

questions.prompt: Which two details matter before taking the suggested middle route?

options.text: Whether every entry requires the same net drive

questions.explanation: The middle route is a teaching option under these conditions, not a mandatory route on every entry.

questions.prompt: Arrange a support read for the wide entry.

options.text: Move on a different useful route

questions.explanation: The supporter must continue checking for changing coverage.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to illustrate a separate middle support route.
questions.explanation: This creates a different lane from F1. Actual route timing and the defender’s movement must still be judged.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 steps into that middle route, what could you change?

options.text: Continue through Gold 2 because the drill named a route
Delay or choose another support lane

questions.explanation: A defender closing a route changes the available options; another route may be equally useful.

questions.prompt: Why should F1 and the supporting forward avoid filling exactly the same lane?
questions.explanation: Different lanes can ask defenders to cover more space, provided the support remains reachable and onside.

questions.prompt: Which space should YOU offer to complement F1’s wide entry?

options.text: The controlled middle route toward the far-post area
The same wide lane beside F1

questions.explanation: The middle route complements F1’s wide lane and gives the carrier a different angle toward the far post; if Gold 2 closes it, keep separation and find the next visible lane.

questions.prompt: Which two checks should precede a middle route?

options.text: Whether the far-post route is automatically clear because F1 is wide

questions.explanation: The defender’s inside position and carrier control determine whether the middle route helps; the bench is unrelated.

questions.prompt: Move YOU inside but below F1 to show a far-post support route.
questions.explanation: The inside-lower spot gives F1 a different lane toward the far post; if Gold 1 closes it, stay connected to the wide carrier.

questions.prompt: Why must the supporting forward avoid filling F1’s exact lane?
questions.explanation: Separate lanes give F1 room and create a second passing angle, while the same lane lets one defender cover both; if the carrier changes direction, re-space.

This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
